title: Fixed lunar cycle terms lowered cross-coast daily high-water correlation at six US gauges in 2011-2025
abstract: We tested whether simple lunar cycle terms reduce daily high-water correlation between opposite US coasts in years not used to fit the terms. We used fixed NOAA CO-OPS data at six gauges. Each outcome was the hourly-based daily maximum minus monthly mean sea level. We fit separate site models in 1996-2010 and tested eight Atlantic-Pacific pairs in 2011-2025. The mean pair correlation fell from 0.458 with calendar-month terms alone to 0.012 with three fixed lunar cycles. The reduction was 0.446, with a conditional 95% three-year block interval of 0.422 to 0.469. Terms at off-frequency periods left the mean at 0.457. Spring-neap terms alone left a mean of 0.356. All six sites had lower test error with the three-cycle model. The result supports a shared lunar signal as an explanation for much of the broad daily correlation in these records. It does not establish a causal share of storm activity, full site independence, or a rare flood result. The package includes the fixed daily table, exact source paths and hashes, fitted terms, test residuals, saved block draws, code, a figure, and source and numerical checks.

display.caption: Mean correlation and eight pair correlations in 2011-2025 after fits in 1996-2010. Bars show conditional 95% three-year block intervals. The off-frequency control has the same number of added terms as the lunar model.

citations.reason: We reuse its verified daily table and NOAA source provenance. We test its proposed lunar explanation with fixed periods and a separate time period for model testing.
Prior tide-gauge work separates extreme sea level and skew surge patterns and shows the role of spring tides. Our daily correlation test has a different scope.
NOAA definitions of lunar cycles, phase inequality, and perigee effects motivate the fixed periods.
Prior geological method uses known lunar periods to model tidal patterns.
NOAA source API. Exact 30 query URLs and source hashes are preserved in source_provenance.json.
